WMU 338 Aerial Ungulate  Survey (2015 -16) 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 338 is a largely conifer forested unit with traditionally medium to low 
densities of moose and other ungulates. The last survey conducted for a moose population estimate was in 
winter of 20 08/09 using the random stratified block methodology . There was no attempt to estimate 
populations of either white-tail or mule deer during previous surveys. Antlered moose are managed on a limited 
entry hunt with an archery only S1 -O31 s eason and a general N1 -N30 season . There is no antlerless moose 
season.  Mule deer (antlered) are also managed through a limited entry hunt N1 -N30 and a general archery only 
S1-O31 season.  White -tailed deer (antlered and antlerless) are managed by a general archery only S1 -O31 
season and a general N1 -N30 season; up until 201 5 two supplemental antlerless tags could also be acquired, 
however, this has currently been reduced to one tag.  
Survey Method 
The objective of this survey was to establish population estimates for moose, white- tailed and mule deer; 
including age and sex classifications where possible.  Transects, up to 10 km in length and oriented north -south, 
were established spatially throughout the WMU at 2 km intervals within a GIS environment.  T ransects were 
randomly select ed until 992 kilometres of survey distance w as achieved.  The survey was then flown using 
distance sampling methodology as described in the Distance Sampling Chapter of the Aerial Ungulate Survey 
Protocol Manual (ESRD, 2014).   
Results 
The survey was completed from January  18-22, 2016. Total ungulates observed were 66 moose, 96 white-tailed 
deer, no mule deer and only 10 elk observed with 42 and 46 moose and white -tailed deer independent groups, 
respectively. Of the 65 moose that were successfully classified, 43 were cows, 10 were calves, and 12 were bulls.  
Due to most white- tailed deer bucks having dropped their antlers, a sex ratio was not possible . Historical and 
current population estimates and species densities are presented in Tables 1 –  2.  Additional effort was given to 
locate elk herds but with limited success, therefore an overall low elk count was obtained. Of the 10  elk 
classified, 6 were cows and 4 were calves.
